552.t: Peter Leitch's duo gig and learning tunes by roots
552.s: Learning obscure tunes for Peter Leitch and his method of learning root movement, chords, then melody.
552.ch: Richmond and arriving in New York
552.q: It’s impossible. As a matter of fact I occasionally play with a great guitarist named Peter Leitch. He has a regular Sunday night gig in New York at a place called Walker’s. Just a duo. And every week he has somebody different. And I do the gig like every couple of months and it’s good for that…

552.t: Tunes you must know at a session
552.s: Rhythm changes, Cherokee, blues; the Giant Steps and It's You or No One stories and Harold Mabern's advice.
552.ch: Richmond and arriving in New York

172.t: Working up tunes from records at rehearsal
172.s: The band took tunes off records, spending a few hours at rehearsal, and played them before rival bands to make hits.

900.s: He describes sitting in at Manassas with a band and learning songs as they were called.
900.q: I have several albums from the Manassas Jazz Festival that I recorded and it’s me learning songs. I mean honest to God. Oh you’re so right. Because I was there and a guy, I forget the guy’s name. He led a band called the Red Onion Jazz Band, and he came up to me and he says, “Hey, Allred” he says,…

312.t: Learning tunes off records and from Paul Parker
312.s: Tunes came from records and Paul Parker's chording, with songs already in their heads.
312.q: Mainly off the records. Or, as happens, somebody might know the melody — well Paul Parker would chord it for us and he’d say this is how it goes, and we’d try and get it and he’d say no, no, that’s wrong, you know, so we’d learn it that way. But for some reason, and I think it’s because of this…

458.t: Learning tunes and faking with Duke Ellington
458.s: Beal learned tunes by playing along with Erroll Garner records; he subbed on a TV show with Duke Ellington, who followed his bass notes on a Tony Bennett tune.
458.ch: Studio work and learning the craft
458.q: Well I started out listening, playing along with records like one of the first records I played with was Erroll Garner, who had a great beat, right? And you could find the bass notes pretty easily. So your ear gets attuned through fitting in what’s going on, and you depend — a lot of times you’ll…

980.t: Learning repertoire and Ellis Marsalis's trick tunes
980.s: Bassists cannot fake tunes; Caine recalls Ellis Marsalis calling unknown tunes at Snug Harbor and the need to accept public humiliation.
980.q: It’s hard. I mean other things that advantage horn players and guitar players have is that you know you can fake your way through the melody and then wait for the other guy to solo, and you can hear it. But yeah, beat one I have to do something. It’s hard I mean there’s a thousand, a million tunes…

958.t: How new tunes are taught to the band by ear
958.s: The band learns songs by playing them for each other, letting Future Man and Victor find their own parts, as with the funk backbeat on 'Sinister Minister'. Time on stage helps; studio prep makes Fleck pushier.
958.ch: Teaching, tradition and the banjo's roots
958.q: A lot of times we don’t even do that. A lot of times it’ll just be a sound check. Like today we’ll get on stage, right now we’re not really working on anything new because we’ve only got a few days left of the trip, but if I’ve got something I’ve been working on I might just start playing it. And…

754.t: 'Fake it, kid': sitting in with visiting tenor players
754.s: On house band gigs with visiting tenors, he learned tunes by faking and following the changes; he says he has faked it for sixty years.
754.q: That’s right, except on those gigs that were tenor, piano and drums. Those were — in those days I used to take my fake books with me to all the gigs because I didn’t know the tunes, but they would never give you a chance to turn the page to get it. They’d say, “Forget it, kid, fake it” you know. So…

998.t: Learning tunes and Ray Brown's 'every key' lesson
998.s: Five tunes a week, practice with Pamela York, Ray Brown's lesson to play in every key, and transcribing Paul Chambers.
998.q: There is no cramming for this exam. You cannot do that. Actually a year ago it was one of those situations where I realized I was really lacking. I would be able to sing tunes, but to remember the changes and stuff, I was just kicking my rear end. So I made a goal that I was going to learn five…

974.t: Learning repertoire from the radio and practicing melodies solo
974.s: He and Bucky Pizzarelli learned standards from the radio; he now practices by playing and accompanying melodies like Donna Lee on solo bass.
974.q: Boy I was speaking to Bucky Pizzarelli about this yesterday. He and I were of a generation, we never sat down and learned music. We heard it on the radio. We heard all the songs on the radio that anybody ever played. They were the pop songs of the day that became the jazz standards of later on. And…

840.t: Building repertoire through after-hours gigs and jam sessions
840.s: He was learning tunes, playing after-hours and at Joe and Tony Morello's house, and calls it lifelong learning.
840.q: Yeah I was starting. I mean I’ve never been what I call a tunesmith, but I was trying to learn tunes and build up repertoire. And like playing that jazz gig after hours. And if I didn’t have a jazz gig I would be out at a guy’s house, some guys, Joe Morello, he’s also

745.t: Memorizing tunes, lyrics and the bandstand look
745.s: Learning tunes by melody, the old timers' advice to learn lyrics, Dylan, and helping each other in the rhythm section; Marino as an ear player.
745.ch: Learning tunes and the dance-gig years
745.q: Well you know off of the melody for sure. People will say a song title to me and I’ll go, “Oh I’m not sure” and I’ll say, “sing it.” And once they start singing the melody I connect. Now that doesn’t hook you up for the bridge necessarily you know. The old timers would tell me, “Learn the lyrics”…

116.t: Learning tunes by ear on the bandstand; Neal Caine and Earl Williams
116.s: Rowe quotes bassist Neal Caine on Marsalis calling unknown tunes; Marsalis recalls learning standards by listening for the form with singer Earl Williams.
116.q: I think I did. I mean I didn’t really teach Neal per se. You know he’s interesting, I met him in St. Louis. He had just finished high school and he was coming to New Orleans. I think he told me to go to Tulane to major in something. I don’t think it was music, but he just kept the musical situation…

756.t: Fake books and Jack Palmer's 400 tunes
756.s: Learning tunes from the old fake book and the card-service system. Palmer checked off about 400 tunes to learn.
756.q: That’s right. Only later did I realize there was a whole system that people bought with drawers and there were like five by eight cards with one tune on each, and you bought them and you had your filing cabinet full of tunes. Someone gave me a ton of those not that long ago. So you would buy this…

1004.t: Learning songs and the illegal fake books
1004.s: Her teacher sold her an illegal fake book; she explains how the cards of melody, lyrics and chords were collected.
1004.q: Oh, well there used to be a service that would send to club date musicians — what we call club date musicians now — all the latest songs. And they were little cards like this and they had the melody and the lyrics and the chords. And somebody, I have no idea who, put them together three to a page.…

600.t: Playing with Thad Jones: no rehearsal, learning his tunes by ear
600.s: Thad Jones gave no instructions; Rydin prepared by learning his songs from records. Rowe asks about Jones leaving the States.
600.q: Yes. Playing with Thad Jones was very special. Because he also didn’t want to rehearse. And the first time I played with him I asked him, “What do you want to play?” “Well, we’ll find out” he said. He didn’t say anything what to play. So we went up on stage and you know he talked to the audience.…

364.t: Learning tunes and the first fake book
364.s: Building repertoire after being caught not knowing tunes, helped by an illegal fake book.
364.ch: Condon's circle and New York scene
364.q: I had several experiences with that. In the beginning I felt hesitant about saying I didn’t know a song I thought I can get by with it. And a lot of them you could. You could kind of fake and figure out. But once in a while you’d get one where and it would be some strange changes in it. And it…

372.t: Learning Tristano's tunes by ear and the small repertoire
372.s: He explains learning lines phrase by phrase, who made harmonies, the tunes' origins on standards, and the band's limited repertoire.
372.ch: The Tristano group and leaving for Kenton
372.q: No. As I have stated in the book Warne and I would pick it up phrase by phrase as he played it and learn the whole tune before writing it down, which is a great way to learn a tune.

473.t: Young trumpeter Don Reinberg and sitting in at Snookie's
473.s: Brushing up his reading with 20-year-old Don Reinberg, a legit player amazed that Jones could play "Stardust" without music; after the show Jones sat in with Earl Hines at Snookie's on 46th Street.
473.q: And then I would go out. Sometimes I would go and sit in with Earl, over on 46th, at Snookie's. You know, just when I'd get off, when the show let out.
